title: Aksum: the great power you were never taught
subtitle: Seventeen centuries ago a kingdom in the Horn of Africa minted gold coins in its own name, raised stone stelae over its rulers and was named among the world's great kingdoms by Mani.

parts.text: Aksum was the principal metropolis of a major polity that arose during the early centuries AD in the highlands of northern Ethiopia and southern Eritrea.
At times its authority extended east across the Red Sea to the Yemeni highlands.
There is no sign of settlement at the site of Aksum itself until the first century AD, and the processes that formed the kingdom remain very poorly understood.

image.alt: Early nineteenth-century engraving of a tall stone obelisk beside a church at Axum, with trees, hills and three small figures in the foreground.
image.caption: 'View of the Obelisk and Church at Axum', an engraving after Henry Salt.

parts.text: A Manichaean text, the Kephalaia, lists four great kingdoms in the world: Babylon and Persia, the Romans, the Axumites and a fourth called Silis, and says that none surpasses them.
A reference overview gives the four as Aksum, Rome, Persia and China.
Other scholars read Silis as China; we have not read their work.

blocks.q: In the Kephalaia, which kingdom is named beside the Romans, the Axumites and Babylon-Persia as one of the world's four great kingdoms?
blocks.explain: The Kephalaia lists the kingdom of Babylon and Persia, of the Romans, of the Axumites and of Silis; reading Silis as China comes from other scholars, and a reference overview names China as the fourth.

parts.text: The first coin issues, dated around AD 270, bear the name of King Endybis.
Aksumite gold coins are found only rarely in Ethiopia and Eritrea but more often overseas, notably in Yemen and India.
The British Museum says that many Aksumite gold coins were traded from Ethiopia to Yemen or India.
That is evidence of a trading kingdom, not of a monopoly, which this page does not claim.

sections.title: A script, stone stelae and a new faith

parts.text: Aksum had its own locally developed Ge'ez script.
Its monolithic stelae are now interpreted as royal grave-markers of the third to fourth centuries.
The towering obelisks were carved from single pieces of stone.

image.alt: A tall slab of grey stone standing inside a small stone building, its surface covered in lines of inscribed letters.
image.caption: The Ezana Stone at Aksum, which carries inscriptions in Greek and Ge'ez.

parts.text: Christianity was formally adopted under King Ezana around AD 340, and the crescent and disc was replaced during his reign by the Christian cross.
The British Museum's timeline gives around AD 350 and a reference overview says the mid-fourth century.
Four of Ezana's inscriptions are written in Greek and Ge'ez.

sections.title: Its reach, and its slow end

blocks.prompt: In which year did Aksum's army invade Yemen at the request of the Byzantine emperor?

parts.text: In 525, according to the Oxford Classical Dictionary.
The army of Axum invaded Yemen in 525 at the request of the Christian Byzantine emperor.
Issue of the coinage ceased during the seventh century.
Phillipson says the conquest of Egypt in 642 effectively cut Aksum's link with long-distance trade, and he also cites environmental stress, including timber loss and soil erosion.
Ethiopian tradition is often read as showing that Aksum survived as a political capital into the tenth century, and its coinage was formerly thought to have continued until then.
A reference overview says its political prominence had dissipated by the end of the first millennium.
So the end was slow and its date depends on what is measured: coins, settlement or tradition.

The Metropolitan Museum and UNESCO pages on Aksum could not be opened (errors 429 and 403) and are not cited; they are the likeliest sources for the Ezana Stone's languages.
Dates for Ezana's conversion differ between sources (about 330 to 350); this page gives Phillipson's and notes the British Museum's.

keyPoints.text: Aksum was the principal metropolis of a major polity that arose in the early centuries AD in the highlands of northern Ethiopia and southern Eritrea; at times its authority reached across the Red Sea to Yemen.
Its first coins, dated around AD 270, bear the name of King Endybis; many of its gold coins were traded to Yemen or India.
Christianity was formally adopted under King Ezana around AD 340, though some sources say about 350.
Coinage ceased in the seventh century, which Phillipson ties to the conquest of Egypt in 642 cutting Aksum off from long-distance trade.
